extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, in-house IP counsel, patent prosecutors, and IP policy practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and case-based criteria for evaluating whether patent claims (especially computer-implemented/system/method claims) are patent‑eligible under §101/Alice (step one: whether claims are directed to an abstract idea; step two: whether there is an inventive concept). Summarizes holdings and explanatory language from recent Federal Circuit and district court decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claims are 'directed to' an abstract idea (e.g., voting/verification/tabulation; selecting certain information, analyzing it using mathematical techniques, and reporting/displaying results; converting geospatial coordinates into natural numbers; entering/transmitting/locating/compressing/storing/displaying data to facilitate buying and selling; collecting/analyzing/manipulating/displaying data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples on the page label such subject matter as abstract: voting and tabulation; mathematical analysis and display of investment data; converting geospatial coordinates; filtering electronic files; organizing or cataloging information; basic economic/business practices implemented on computers. The inquiry focuses on the 'focus of the claims' and whether that focus is an abstract idea rather than a physical-realm improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of inventive concept (Alice step two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims lack an 'inventive concept' if they recite nothing more than conventional computer components or generic computer-implemented steps to carry out the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page repeatedly finds claims deficient because they 'required only generic computers to carry out the claimed method,' 'simply require generic computer-implemented steps,' or 'just already available computers, with their already available basic functions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting generic computer hardware, field-of-use limitations, servers/clients, GUIs, or 'parallel processing' without claiming anything different from existing systems does not render claims patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple decisions state that mere inclusion of a 'processor,' 'receiver,' server/client, or conventional architecture is inadequate; claim must specify an improvement other than generic computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/nonobviousness (§§102/103) is not §101 inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not enough for subject-matter eligibility that claimed techniques be novel and nonobvious under §§102 and 103; novelty alone does not satisfy Alice step two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: 'it is not enough for subject-matter eligibility that claimed techniques be novel and nonobvious in light of prior art, passing must under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 and 103.' Advances that lie entirely in the realm of abstract ideas are ineligible even if novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement must be rooted in computer technology or physical realm
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that present an improvement 'rooted in computer technology' or that 'improve[d] the efficient functioning of computers' can be patent eligible; mere presentation of information is not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data Engine holding: tab claims were not abstract because they 'improved the efficient functioning of computers' by allowing convenient navigation. Conversely, claims that only improve presentation of information are not improvements 'rooted in computer technology.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconventional feature that is the abstract idea cannot supply inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: An unconventional feature does not provide an inventive concept if that feature 'is the abstract idea itself, or the use thereof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From BSG Tech: even an 'unconventional feature' cannot make an abstract idea patent eligible when the unconventionality is of the abstract idea rather than a technological implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read claims as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The eligibility inquiry requires that the claims be read 'as a whole' rather than dissected into individual elements in isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited explicitly in Data Engine Techs. 'The eligibility inquiry requires that the claims be read as a whole.' This affects both step one (directed to) and step two (inventive concept) analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventionality / well-understood, routine, previously known
rubrics_metrics.description: If claim limitations are well-understood, routine, and previously known to the industry, they do not supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts repeatedly reject assertions of inventive concept where the steps are 'conventional,' 'functional in nature,' or 'merely conventional steps that are well-understood, routine, and previously known to the industry.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that merely implement human practices on computers
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that simply recite longstanding human practices (e.g., budgeting, cataloging, upselling, auctions, business transactions, teaching) as implemented on a computer are directed to abstract ideas and lack inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many district court holdings treat computerized implementations of traditional human/commercial practices as abstract—e.g., loyalty award conversion, mortgage paydown strategies, auctions, broadcasting content, crowdfunding, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concern and overly broad claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that could 'foreclose fields of research beyond the actual invention' or broadly preempt concrete applications of an idea weigh against eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amdocs and other cases warn that overly general claims reciting conventional operations in broad terms risk invalidation because they could preempt too much ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual disputes & role of extrinsic evidence at pleading stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual allegations or extrinsic evidence can give rise to disputes that may preclude resolution of eligibility at the pleading stage, but conclusory legal assertions or unsupported expert declarations are not dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interval Licensing: extrinsic evidence can create factual dispute; courts have resolved §101 on Rule 12(b)(6)/(c) where undisputed facts require holding of ineligibility. However, district courts are 'not bound to accept as true' conclusory legal assertions or mere expert declarations of alleged advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim language that 'simply instructs the practitioner to implement the abstract idea on a generic computer' is invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that effectively tell a practitioner to perform an abstract idea using a generic computer are insufficient to pass Alice step two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., diet behavior modification system and others were invalidated for doing no more than instructing implementation of an abstract idea on a generic computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific technical improvements vs. information-processing improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that effect a specific technical improvement in how computers operate are more likely eligible than claims that merely improve abstract information-processing or presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data Engine's 'flip through' spreadsheet navigation produced a finding of non-abstract because it improved computer functionality; by contrast, claims that merely 'present the graphic user interface as merely a generic computer component' failed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining abstract ideas does not necessarily make them eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining two or more abstract ideas does not by itself bring a patent within §101; merely aggregating abstract concepts is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District court rejected argument that combining two or three abstract ideas met Alice, noting no authority that mere combination converts ineligible subject matter into eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that 'identify and store' or 'create base and new versions and determine changes' are routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite routine data-keeping steps (creating base version, creating new version, determining changes) are likely directed to an abstract idea and lack inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data Engine and other cases found such spreadsheet-tracking/record-keeping claims ineligible because they recited generic, routine steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert/specialized terminology does not overcome genericity absent specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Using specialized-sounding words or invoking 'technology used to improve communications' is insufficient without claim limitations describing how the technology is different from conventional practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have rejected 'conclusory legal assertions' and expert declarations that merely assert advantages or novelty without tying limitations to specific technological improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility can be resolved on motion where undisputed facts require it
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility 'may be, and frequently has been, resolved on a Rule 12(b)(6) or (c) motion where the undisputed facts... require a holding of ineligibility under the substantive standards of law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple cases cited grant motions to dismiss or judgment on pleadings applying Alice when the asserted claims and undisputed facts show the claims are directed to abstract ideas with no inventive concept.
